q: Displacement of a body is best described as:
o: The straight-line change in position from the initial to the final point, with direction
The total length of the path followed by the body
The total length of the path divided by the time taken
The shortest distance between two points, with no direction
x: Displacement is a vector: the change in position, drawn as a straight line from start to finish with a direction. The total path length is distance, a scalar.

q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
x: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Distance, speed and time have magnitude only and are scalars.

q: An athlete runs exactly one lap of a 400 m circular track and stops at the starting point. The distance covered and the magnitude of the displacement are:
x: The path length is 400 m, but the final position is the same as the initial position, so the displacement is zero.

q: A boy walks 3 m due east and then 4 m due north. The magnitude of his displacement is:
x: The two legs are at right angles, so displacement = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 m. 7 m is the distance travelled, not the displacement.

q: A particle moves along a semicircle of radius 7 m from one end of a diameter to the other. Taking π = 22/7, the ratio of distance travelled to magnitude of displacement is:
x: Distance = πr = 22 m; displacement = diameter = 14 m. Ratio 22 : 14 = 11 : 7.

q: Which statement about distance and displacement is correct?
o: Distance can be negative if the body moves backwards
Displacement always equals the distance travelled
Displacement depends on the actual path taken between two points
The magnitude of displacement can never be greater than the distance travelled
x: The straight line between two points is the shortest path, so |displacement| ≤ distance. Displacement depends only on the start and end points, not on the path; distance is never negative.

q: A particle on the x-axis moves from x = +3 m to x = −5 m. Its displacement is:
x: Displacement = final position − initial position = (−5) − (+3) = −8 m, i.e. 8 m in the negative x-direction.

q: A particle moves at constant speed around a circle of radius r. After it has covered one quarter of the circle, the magnitude of its displacement is:
x: The start and end points are two radii at 90°, so displacement = √(r² + r²) = r√2. πr/2 is the arc length (distance), and 2r would be the displacement after half a circle.

q: A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. It bounces and is caught at the top of its bounce, 5 m above the ground. The displacement of the ball is:
x: The ball starts 20 m up and ends 5 m up, so its position has changed by 15 m downward. 25 m is the distance travelled (20 m down + 5 m up).

q: The magnitude of a body's displacement equals the distance it travels when the body:
o: Moves along a circular path at constant speed
Moves in a straight line without reversing its direction
x: Only for straight-line motion in one direction is the path length equal to the straight-line separation of start and end. Any curve or reversal makes the distance larger.

q: Average velocity is defined as:
o: Total displacement divided by total time taken
Total distance travelled divided by total time
Change in velocity divided by time taken
The final velocity divided by two
x: Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. Total distance ÷ total time is average speed, and change in velocity ÷ time is acceleration.

q: The direction of a body's average velocity over a time interval is always the same as the direction of its:
x: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time, and time is a positive scalar, so average velocity points the same way as the displacement.

q: A car moves 60 km in the first hour and then 60 km in the next 2 hours along the same straight road in the same direction. Its average velocity for the whole journey is:
x: Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time = 120 km ÷ 3 h = 40 km h⁻¹. 45 km h⁻¹ is the wrong method of averaging the two speeds (60 and 30).

q: A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track in 50 s and finishes where she started. Her average velocity for the lap is:
x: Her displacement over the lap is zero, so average velocity = 0 ÷ 50 s = 0. Her average speed, 400 ÷ 50 = 8 m s⁻¹, is not zero.

q: A car travels from town X to town Y at 40 km h⁻¹ and returns along the same road to X at 60 km h⁻¹. For the whole round trip, its average speed and average velocity are:
x: For equal distances d: time = d/40 + d/60 = d/24, so average speed = 2d ÷ (d/24) = 48 km h⁻¹. The car returns to X, so displacement and average velocity are zero. 50 km h⁻¹ is the simple mean, which is wrong here.

q: A body moves along a straight line in one direction at 20 m s⁻¹ for the first half of the total time and at 30 m s⁻¹ for the second half. Its average velocity is:
x: For equal times t: displacement = 20t + 30t = 50t in a total time 2t, so average velocity = 25 m s⁻¹. 24 m s⁻¹ would be the answer for equal halves of the distance, not of the time.

q: A cyclist rides 300 m due east in 60 s and then 100 m due west in 40 s. Her average velocity for the whole motion is:
x: Net displacement = 300 − 100 = 200 m east; total time = 100 s. Average velocity = 200 ÷ 100 = 2 m s⁻¹ east. 4 m s⁻¹ is the average speed (400 m ÷ 100 s).

q: A girl walks 3 m east and then 4 m north, taking 10 s in total. The magnitude of her average velocity is:
x: Displacement = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m, so average velocity = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 m s⁻¹. 0.7 m s⁻¹ is her average speed (7 m ÷ 10 s).

q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s along a straight road. Using its average velocity, the distance it covers in this time is:
x: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (0 + 20) ÷ 2 = 10 m s⁻¹, so distance = 10 × 10 = 100 m. 200 m wrongly uses the final velocity for the whole time.

q: Which statement is correct for any motion over a given time interval?
o: Average velocity is always equal to average speed
Average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity
Average velocity can be non-zero even when the displacement is zero
Average speed is zero whenever the body returns to its starting point
x: Distance is never less than the magnitude of displacement, so average speed ≥ |average velocity|. If displacement is zero, average velocity is zero, but average speed is not.

q: The slope (gradient) of a displacement–time graph gives the:
x: Slope = change in displacement ÷ change in time = velocity. The slope of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.

q: The area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis represents the:
x: Area under a v–t graph = velocity × time = displacement. The slope of the v–t graph, not its area, gives acceleration.

q: The displacement–time graph of a body is a straight line parallel to the time axis. The body is:
x: A horizontal displacement–time line means the displacement does not change with time, so the slope (velocity) is zero: the body is at rest.

q: The displacement–time graph of a body is a straight line sloping upwards from the origin. The body is moving with:
x: A straight line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant (uniform). A curved displacement–time graph would be needed for acceleration.

q: A body's displacement–time graph is a curve whose slope becomes steeper and steeper with time. This shows that the body:
o: Is slowing down to a stop
x: The slope of a displacement–time graph is velocity; a slope that keeps increasing means the velocity keeps increasing, so the body is accelerating.

q: A displacement–time graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (4 s, 20 m). The velocity of the body is:
x: Velocity = slope = 20 m ÷ 4 s = 5 m s⁻¹. 0.2 m s⁻¹ is the inverted ratio (4 ÷ 20).

q: The velocity–time graph of a car is a horizontal line at 10 m s⁻¹ from t = 0 to t = 5 s. The displacement of the car in this time is:
o: Zero, since the graph is horizontal
x: Displacement = area under the v–t graph = 10 m s⁻¹ × 5 s = 50 m. A horizontal v–t line means zero acceleration, not zero displacement.

q: The displacement–time graphs of two bodies are straight lines making angles of 30° and 60° with the time axis (same scales on both). Given tan 30° = 1/√3 and tan 60° = √3, the ratio of their velocities is:
x: Velocity = slope = tan θ, so v₁ : v₂ = (1/√3) : √3 = 1 : 3. 1 : 2 is the ratio of the angles, which is not the ratio of slopes.

q: A displacement–time graph rises as a straight line from 0 m to 10 m between t = 0 and t = 2 s, then stays horizontal until t = 5 s. The average velocity over the 5 s is:
x: Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time = 10 m ÷ 5 s = 2 m s⁻¹. 5 m s⁻¹ is only the velocity during the first 2 s.

q: On a velocity–time graph, a car's velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 20 m s⁻¹ in 4 s and then stays at 20 m s⁻¹ for a further 6 s. The total displacement in the 10 s is:
x: Area = triangle + rectangle = ½ × 4 × 20 + 6 × 20 = 40 + 120 = 160 m. 200 m wrongly treats the whole 10 s at 20 m s⁻¹.

q: Acceleration is defined as the:
o: Change of speed per unit distance
x: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken; its SI unit is m s⁻². Rate of change of displacement is velocity.

q: A car speeds up uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
x: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (30 − 10) ÷ 5 = 4 m s⁻². 6 m s⁻² uses the final velocity only (30 ÷ 5).

q: A velocity–time graph is a straight line falling from 20 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to zero at t = 4 s. The acceleration of the body is:
x: Acceleration = slope = (0 − 20) ÷ 4 = −5 m s⁻². The negative sign shows the body is slowing down (deceleration of 5 m s⁻²).

q: A stone moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which statement is correct?
o: It is accelerating, because the direction of its velocity keeps changing
It has no acceleration, because its speed is constant
It is accelerating only if its speed increases
Its acceleration is along its direction of motion
x: Velocity is a vector; a change in direction alone is a change in velocity, so the stone accelerates (towards the centre), even at constant speed.

q: A body moves in the positive x-direction while its acceleration points in the negative x-direction. The speed of the body:
x: When acceleration is opposite to velocity, the velocity decreases in magnitude, so the body slows down.

q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. The distance it covers is:
x: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 5² = 25 m. 50 m comes from forgetting the factor ½.

q: A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly and stops in a distance of 40 m. The magnitude of its deceleration is:
x: v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 20² − 2a × 40, so a = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m s⁻². 10 m s⁻² comes from forgetting the factor 2.

q: A stone is dropped from rest from a tall tower. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its velocity after 3 s is:
x: v = u + gt = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m s⁻¹. 45 is the distance fallen in metres (½ × 10 × 3²), not the velocity.

q: In which situation does a body have zero velocity but a non-zero acceleration?
o: A car moving at constant velocity on a straight road
A book lying at rest on a table
A train moving at steady speed on a straight track
A ball at the highest point of its vertical upward throw
x: At the top of its flight the ball is momentarily at rest, but gravity still gives it an acceleration of g downward. In the other cases acceleration is zero.

q: The dimensions of acceleration are:
x: Acceleration = velocity ÷ time = (L T⁻¹) ÷ T = [LT⁻²]. [LT⁻¹] is velocity and [MLT⁻²] is force.

q: A body is said to have uniform acceleration when its:
o: Velocity stays the same in all intervals of time
Displacement changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time
Velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time
Velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals of time
x: Uniform acceleration means a constant rate of change of velocity: equal changes of velocity in equal times. Unequal changes mean variable acceleration.

q: For a body moving in a straight line, the velocity–time graphs for uniform and for variable acceleration are, respectively:
o: A curve and a straight sloping line
A straight sloping line and a curve
A horizontal line and a straight sloping line
A straight sloping line and a horizontal line
x: Uniform acceleration gives a constant slope, so the v–t graph is a straight sloping line; variable acceleration gives a changing slope, so the graph is curved. A horizontal line means zero acceleration.

q: Which motion is the standard example of uniform acceleration?
o: A car moving through busy city traffic
A body falling freely near the Earth's surface with no air resistance
A stone whirled in a circle at constant speed
A parachutist falling at terminal velocity
x: Near the Earth's surface, a freely falling body has a constant acceleration g. City traffic gives variable acceleration, circular motion has a changing direction of acceleration, and terminal velocity means zero acceleration.

q: The velocity of a body, read at 1 s intervals, is given in four cases below. Which set shows uniform acceleration?
x: In 2, 5, 8, 11 m s⁻¹ the velocity rises by the same 3 m s⁻¹ every second, so the acceleration is uniform (3 m s⁻²). In the other sets the increases are unequal.

q: The equations of motion v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as can be used only when the body moves in a straight line with:
x: These equations are derived assuming the acceleration is constant. For variable acceleration they do not apply.

q: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. The distances it covers in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds are in the ratio:
x: Total distances after 1, 2, 3 s are proportional to 1, 4, 9 (s = ½at²). Distances in each separate second are 1, 4 − 1, 9 − 4 = 1 : 3 : 5. 1 : 4 : 9 is the ratio of total distances.

q: A car starts from rest with uniform acceleration and covers 20 m in the first 2 s. The total distance it covers in the first 4 s is:
x: From rest, s = ½at², so s ∝ t². Doubling the time multiplies the distance by 4: 4 × 20 = 80 m. 40 m wrongly assumes s ∝ t.

q: The velocity–time graph of a car is a curve that rises but becomes less and less steep as time passes. This shows that the car's:
o: Speed is decreasing while acceleration is constant
Speed and acceleration are both constant
Speed is increasing while its acceleration is decreasing
Acceleration is increasing while speed is constant
x: A rising v–t graph means velocity is increasing; a falling slope means the acceleration is getting smaller. This is variable acceleration.

q: A body moving with uniform acceleration has a velocity of 10 m s⁻¹ at one instant and 30 m s⁻¹ 4 s later. The distance it covers in these 4 s is:
x: With uniform acceleration, average velocity = (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20 m s⁻¹, so distance = 20 × 4 = 80 m. 120 m uses the final velocity for the whole time.

q: When a body moves with variable acceleration, its acceleration at a particular instant is given by the:
o: Slope of the straight line joining the start and end points of the velocity–time graph
Area under the velocity–time graph up to that instant
Slope of the tangent to the velocity–time graph at that instant
Velocity at that instant divided by the time elapsed
x: Instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the tangent at that point. The slope of the chord joining two points gives average acceleration, and the area gives displacement.

q: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of:
x: The first law states that a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a net force acts; this tendency is inertia, so it is called the law of inertia.

q: When a moving bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers tend to fall forward. This is due to:
o: A forward force exerted by the brakes on the passengers
The reaction force of the floor pushing them forward
Gravity acting more strongly during braking
The inertia of motion of their bodies
x: The bus slows, but the passengers' bodies tend to keep moving forward because of inertia (first law). No extra forward force acts on them.

q: A car moves at a steady 20 m s⁻¹ along a straight, level road with its engine running. The net force on the car is:
o: Equal to the forward force of the engine
Equal to the weight of the car
x: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first and second laws the net force is zero: the forward driving force is balanced by friction and air resistance.

q: A 50 kg person stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s⁻². Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the reading of the scale is:
x: R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 50 × (10 + 2) = 600 N. 400 N would be for a lift accelerating downward.

q: A 50 kg person stands on a scale in a lift moving downward at a constant velocity. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the scale reads:
x: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the normal reaction equals the weight: R = mg = 50 × 10 = 500 N. The direction of motion does not matter, only the acceleration.

q: The cable of a lift breaks and the lift falls freely. A person standing on a weighing scale inside the lift would read:
x: In free fall the lift's acceleration is g downward, so R = m(g − a) = m(g − g) = 0: the person is apparently weightless.

q: A block slides down a smooth (frictionless) plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and sin 30° = 0.5, its acceleration down the plane is:
x: The component of weight along the plane is mg sin θ, so a = g sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m s⁻². 8.7 m s⁻² wrongly uses g cos 30°.

q: A 2 kg block rests on a smooth plane inclined at 60° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and cos 60° = 0.5, the normal force of the plane on the block is:
x: Perpendicular to the plane there is no acceleration, so R = mg cos θ = 2 × 10 × 0.5 = 10 N. 17.3 N wrongly uses mg sin 60°.

q: Blocks of mass 3 kg and 2 kg lie on a smooth horizontal surface, joined by a light string. A horizontal force of 10 N pulls the 3 kg block, so both move together. The tension in the string is:
x: For the whole system a = 10 ÷ (3 + 2) = 2 m s⁻². The string alone pulls the 2 kg block, so T = 2 × 2 = 4 N. 6 N is the net force on the 3 kg block, not the tension.

q: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang from the two ends of a light string passing over a smooth, light pulley. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the acceleration of the masses is:
x: a = (m₁ − m₂)g ÷ (m₁ + m₂) = (3 − 2) × 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m s⁻². 10 m s⁻² would be free fall, which ignores the opposing mass.

q: In terms of momentum, Newton's second law states that the net force on a body is equal to its:
o: Change in momentum per unit distance
x: F = Δp ÷ Δt: net force equals the rate of change of momentum. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.

q: The area under a force–time graph for a body represents the:
o: Impulse, equal to the change in momentum
x: Area = force × time = impulse, and by Newton's second law impulse equals the change in momentum. Work is the area under a force–displacement graph.

q: Impulse has the same SI unit as:
x: Impulse = F × t, measured in N s; and 1 N s = 1 kg m s⁻¹, the unit of momentum. This is because impulse equals the change in momentum.

q: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 10 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest in 0.1 s. The average force needed to stop it is:
x: F = Δp ÷ Δt = (0.5 × 10) ÷ 0.1 = 5 ÷ 0.1 = 50 N. 5 N is the change in momentum, not the force.

q: A 0.2 kg ball strikes a wall at right angles at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 10 m s⁻¹. The contact time is 0.05 s. The average force exerted by the wall on the ball is:
x: The velocity reverses, so the size of Δp = 0.2 × (10 + 10) = 4 kg m s⁻¹, so F = 4 ÷ 0.05 = 80 N. 40 N forgets that the velocity reverses; zero wrongly assumes equal speeds mean no change in momentum.

q: A fielder pulls his hands backwards while catching a fast cricket ball. This reduces the force on his hands because it:
o: Increases the time taken to stop the ball
Reduces the change in momentum of the ball
Increases the mass of the ball
Reduces the time taken to stop the ball
x: The change in momentum is fixed (from mv to zero). Since F = Δp ÷ Δt, spreading it over a longer time gives a smaller force.

q: A constant force of 20 N acts for 0.5 s on a 2 kg body initially at rest. The final velocity of the body is:
x: Impulse = F t = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N s = change in momentum, so v = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m s⁻¹. 10 m s⁻¹ forgets to divide by the mass.

q: Equal impulses are given to two bodies at rest, of masses m and 2m. The ratio of their final speeds (mass m : mass 2m) is:
x: Equal impulse gives equal momentum, mv = constant, so speed ∝ 1/m. The lighter body moves twice as fast: 2 : 1.

q: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second, each of mass 0.02 kg, with a speed of 500 m s⁻¹. The average force needed to hold the gun in place is:
x: Momentum given to bullets per second = n m v = 10 × 0.02 × 500 = 100 kg m s⁻²; by F = Δp ÷ Δt the gun needs a 100 N force. 10 N is the momentum of one bullet.

q: According to Newton's third law, an action force and its reaction force are:
o: Equal and opposite and act on the same body
Equal and opposite and act on different bodies
Unequal and act in the same direction
Equal and act in the same direction on different bodies
x: Third law forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and act on two different bodies; that is why they never cancel each other.

q: Action and reaction forces do not cancel each other out because they:
x: Forces cancel only when they act on the same body. Action and reaction act on two different bodies, so each can accelerate its own body.

q: A book rests on a table. By Newton's third law, the reaction to the Earth's gravitational pull on the book is the:
o: Gravitational pull of the book on the Earth
Upward push of the table on the book
Downward push of the book on the table
x: The Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls the Earth up with an equal force. The table's push balances the weight but is a different interaction, not its third-law pair.

q: The law of conservation of linear momentum applies to a system of bodies when:
o: The bodies move with constant speed
No net external force acts on the system
Only gravity acts on each body
x: Momentum of a system is conserved when it is isolated, i.e. the net external force is zero. Internal forces cancel in pairs by the third law. Kinetic energy need not be conserved.

q: Two bodies interact only with each other for a short time. By Newton's third law, the changes in their momenta are:
o: Equal in magnitude and in the same direction
Unequal, the lighter body changing more
Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
x: The bodies exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so the impulses (F × t) are equal and opposite. Hence the momentum changes cancel and total momentum is conserved.

q: A rocket in space moves forward because:
o: The exhaust gases push against the air behind the rocket
Gravity becomes weaker as the rocket rises
The rocket pushes against the launch pad all the time
The rocket pushes on the exhaust gases backward and the gases push the rocket forward
x: By the third law the rocket pushes the gases backward and the gases push the rocket forward with an equal force; equivalently, total momentum is conserved. No air is needed.

q: In a head-on collision between a heavy truck and a small car, which statement is correct?
o: The truck exerts a larger force on the car than the car exerts on the truck
Both experience forces of equal magnitude, but the car has the larger acceleration
Both experience equal forces and equal accelerations
The car exerts a larger force because it decelerates more
x: By the third law the forces are equal and opposite. Since a = F/m, the lighter car has the much larger acceleration.

q: The total momentum of an isolated system of two bodies is 10 kg m s⁻¹ due east. After the bodies push on each other, the total momentum of the system is:
x: Internal forces are third-law pairs and cancel, so with no external force the total momentum remains unchanged in size and direction: 10 kg m s⁻¹ east.

q: When a man jumps from a small boat onto the shore, the boat moves away from the shore. This is because:
o: The water pushes the boat backward
The man pushes the boat backward and the boat pushes him forward with an equal force
The man's weight acts backward on the boat
The boat has more inertia than the man
x: The man's push on the boat and the boat's push on him are a third-law pair; the boat gains backward momentum equal in size to the man's forward momentum.

q: In an inelastic collision between two bodies, with no external force:
o: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
x: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound or deformation.

q: A collision is called perfectly inelastic when the colliding bodies:
o: Bounce apart with no loss of kinetic energy
Come to rest without any change in momentum
Stick together and move with a common velocity
x: In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together, so they move with one common velocity; the loss of kinetic energy is the maximum possible while momentum is conserved.

q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides with a 1 kg trolley at rest, and they stick together. Their common velocity is:
x: Momentum: 2 × 6 + 1 × 0 = (2 + 1)v, so v = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m s⁻¹. 3 m s⁻¹ would be the simple average of 6 and 0.

q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides with a 1 kg trolley at rest and they move off together at 4 m s⁻¹. The kinetic energy lost in the collision is:
x: KE before = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J; KE after = ½ × 3 × 4² = 24 J. Loss = 36 − 24 = 12 J. Zero would only be true for an elastic collision.

q: A 1 kg ball moving at 5 m s⁻¹ collides head-on and perfectly elastically with an identical ball at rest. After the collision the velocities of the first and second balls are:
x: In a 1-D elastic collision between equal masses, the velocities are exchanged: the moving ball stops and the other moves off at 5 m s⁻¹. Equal shared velocities would mean an inelastic collision.

q: A 3 kg body moving at 4 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a 1 kg body moving at 4 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. They stick together. Their common velocity is:
o: 2 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of the 3 kg body
4 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of the 3 kg body
2 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of the 1 kg body
3 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of the 3 kg body
x: Total momentum = 3 × 4 − 1 × 4 = 8 kg m s⁻¹ in the 3 kg body's direction; v = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m s⁻¹ in that direction.

q: A very heavy body moving at speed u collides head-on and perfectly elastically with a very light body at rest. The light body moves off with a speed of about:
x: For m₁ ≫ m₂, v₂ = 2m₁u ÷ (m₁ + m₂) ≈ 2u. The heavy body continues at almost u, and the relative speed of separation (2u − u = u) equals the speed of approach.

q: A light rubber ball strikes a massive fixed wall head-on at speed v. If the collision is perfectly elastic, the ball:
o: Rebounds with speed v in the opposite direction
x: For a very light body hitting a very massive body at rest, v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u ÷ (m₁ + m₂) ≈ −u: it bounces back with the same speed, so no kinetic energy is lost.

q: A 1 kg ball moving at 6 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on perfectly elastic collision with a 2 kg ball at rest. Taking the original direction as positive, the velocities of the 1 kg and 2 kg balls afterwards are:
x: v₁ = (1 − 2) × 6 ÷ 3 = −2 m s⁻¹; v₂ = 2 × 1 × 6 ÷ 3 = 4 m s⁻¹. Check: momentum −2 + 8 = 6 and KE 2 + 16 = 18 J, both as before. The other pairs conserve momentum but not kinetic energy.

q: A shell at rest explodes into several fragments. Just after the explosion, the total momentum of all the fragments is:
o: Equal to the total kinetic energy of the fragments
Greater than zero, in the direction of the largest fragment
Equal to the momentum of the largest fragment
x: The explosion forces are internal, so total momentum is conserved. It was zero before (shell at rest), so the vector sum of the fragments' momenta is zero.

q: A 4 kg gun fires a 20 g bullet horizontally at 400 m s⁻¹. The recoil speed of the gun is:
x: Total momentum stays zero: 4V = 0.02 × 400 = 8, so V = 2 m s⁻¹. 20 m s⁻¹ comes from using 20 g as 0.2 kg.

q: Two skaters of mass 40 kg and 60 kg stand at rest on smooth ice and push each other apart. The 60 kg skater moves off at 2 m s⁻¹. The speed of the 40 kg skater is:
x: Momentum before is zero, so 40v = 60 × 2 = 120, giving v = 3 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. 1.3 m s⁻¹ uses the masses the wrong way round.

q: A bomb at rest explodes into two pieces whose masses are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their speeds (lighter : heavier) is:
x: The two pieces have equal and opposite momenta, m₁v₁ = m₂v₂, so v₁ : v₂ = m₂ : m₁ = 2 : 1. The lighter piece moves faster.

q: A bomb at rest explodes into two pieces whose masses are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their kinetic energies (lighter : heavier) is:
x: Both pieces have the same magnitude of momentum p, and KE = p² ÷ 2m, so KE ∝ 1/m: ratio 2 : 1. 4 : 1 comes from squaring the speed ratio but forgetting the mass.

q: Which statement about an explosion of a body that was initially at rest is correct?
o: Total momentum stays zero while total kinetic energy increases
Momentum and kinetic energy are both unchanged
Total momentum increases while kinetic energy stays zero
Total momentum and total kinetic energy both increase
x: Internal forces cannot change the total momentum, so it stays zero. Chemical or stored energy is converted into kinetic energy, so the total kinetic energy increases.

q: A 3 kg body moving at 4 m s⁻¹ explodes into two pieces of 1.5 kg each. One piece comes to rest just after the explosion. The velocity of the other piece is:
x: Momentum before = 3 × 4 = 12 kg m s⁻¹, all carried by the moving piece: 1.5v = 12, so v = 8 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.

q: When a gun fires a bullet, the gun recoils with a much smaller speed than the bullet because:
o: The gun receives a smaller force than the bullet
The momentum of the gun is much smaller than that of the bullet
The gun gains kinetic energy equal to that of the bullet
The gun and the bullet gain equal magnitudes of momentum, and the gun has a much larger mass
x: Total momentum stays zero, so the gun's momentum equals the bullet's in magnitude. With a much larger mass, the gun's speed (p ÷ m) is much smaller. The forces on them are equal.

q: A 5 kg rifle fires a 10 g bullet. The rifle recoils at 0.8 m s⁻¹. The speed of the bullet is:
x: 0.01 × v = 5 × 0.8 = 4, so v = 4 ÷ 0.01 = 400 m s⁻¹. 4000 m s⁻¹ comes from writing 10 g as 0.001 kg.

q: In a perfectly elastic head-on collision between two bodies, the relative speed of approach is:
o: Equal to the relative speed of separation
Greater than the relative speed of separation
Less than the relative speed of separation
x: For a perfectly elastic collision in one dimension, the bodies separate with the same relative speed with which they approached.

q: Which equation holds for a perfectly elastic collision in one dimension, where u₁, u₂ are velocities before and v₁, v₂ are velocities after?
x: Relative velocity of approach (u₁ − u₂) equals relative velocity of separation (v₂ − v₁). This comes from combining conservation of momentum and kinetic energy.

q: Ball P moving at 5 m s⁻¹ catches up with ball Q moving at 2 m s⁻¹ in the same direction along the same line. The collision is perfectly elastic. Their relative speed of separation is:
x: Relative speed of approach = 5 − 2 = 3 m s⁻¹ (same direction, so subtract). In a perfectly elastic collision the speed of separation is also 3 m s⁻¹.

q: Two balls move towards each other along a line at 3 m s⁻¹ and 4 m s⁻¹ and collide perfectly elastically. Afterwards, the speed of one ball relative to the other is:
x: Moving towards each other, the speed of approach is 3 + 4 = 7 m s⁻¹, so in a perfectly elastic collision they separate at 7 m s⁻¹ relative to each other.

q: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the relative speed of separation of the two bodies is:
o: Equal to the relative speed of approach
Twice the relative speed of approach
Half the relative speed of approach
x: In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and move with the same velocity, so they do not separate at all: relative speed of separation is zero.

q: In a one-dimensional collision the relative speed of approach is 8 m s⁻¹ and the relative speed of separation is 5 m s⁻¹. No external force acts. The collision is:
o: Impossible, since momentum cannot then be conserved
Inelastic, with momentum conserved but some kinetic energy lost
x: The bodies separate more slowly than they approached but they do separate, so the collision is inelastic (not perfectly inelastic): momentum is conserved and some kinetic energy is lost.

q: A ball dropped from a height h hits a hard, fixed floor. If the collision with the floor is perfectly elastic, the ball rebounds to a height of:
x: The floor is fixed, so the speed of separation equals the speed of approach: the ball leaves with the same speed it arrived with and so rises back to the same height h.

q: A ball moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides head-on, perfectly elastically, with a second ball at rest. After the collision the first ball moves on in the same direction at 1 m s⁻¹. The velocity of the second ball is:
x: Speed of approach = 6 − 0 = 6 m s⁻¹ = speed of separation, so v₂ − 1 = 6 and v₂ = 7 m s⁻¹. 5 m s⁻¹ wrongly subtracts the first ball's velocity.

q: Ball P moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits ball Q moving at 1 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. The collision is perfectly elastic and afterwards P moves on at 2 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. The velocity of Q afterwards is:
x: Speed of approach = 4 − 1 = 3 m s⁻¹, so v_Q − 2 = 3 and v_Q = 5 m s⁻¹. 3 m s⁻¹ is the relative speed, not Q's velocity.

q: Projectile motion is an example of:
o: One-dimensional motion along a straight line
Two-dimensional motion in a vertical plane
Circular motion in a horizontal plane
x: A projectile moves forward and up or down at the same time, so its motion has a horizontal and a vertical part. Both lie in one vertical plane, which makes it two-dimensional motion.

q: A ball is thrown at an angle to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, in which plane does the whole of its motion take place?
o: The horizontal plane through the point of launch
A plane perpendicular to its initial velocity
The vertical plane that contains its initial velocity
A plane that keeps changing during the flight
x: The initial velocity and the only force (weight, acting straight down) both lie in the vertical plane containing the initial velocity. Nothing pushes the ball out of that plane, so it stays in it.

q: Why is the motion of a projectile two-dimensional rather than three-dimensional?
o: Its horizontal velocity is zero throughout the flight
Air resistance keeps it moving in a single plane
Gravity acts horizontally and cancels any sideways motion
Its initial velocity and its weight lie in one vertical plane, so no sideways velocity develops
x: With no force acting perpendicular to the vertical plane of launch, no velocity component can develop in that direction. Gravity acts vertically, not horizontally, and the horizontal velocity is not zero.

q: The motion of a projectile can be treated as a combination of:
o: Uniform acceleration horizontally and uniform velocity vertically
Uniform velocity both horizontally and vertically
Uniform velocity horizontally and uniform acceleration vertically
Uniform acceleration both horizontally and vertically
x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity is constant. Vertically the weight gives a constant acceleration g downward.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of projectile motion?
o: A car moving round a circular track at constant speed
A football kicked up into the air
A bullet fired horizontally from the top of a cliff
A javelin thrown by an athlete
x: A projectile moves freely under gravity alone after launch. The car is kept on a circular path by friction from the road in a horizontal plane, so it is not a projectile.

q: To give the position of a projectile at any instant, relative to its point of launch, you need:
o: Its horizontal distance and its vertical height
Its horizontal distance, its height and a sideways distance
x: The motion lies in one vertical plane, so two coordinates (x horizontally and y vertically) fix the position. No sideways coordinate is needed because there is no sideways motion.

q: A ball is launched from the ground with speed v at an angle θ above the horizontal. For which value of θ is its motion one-dimensional instead of two-dimensional?
x: At 90° the ball has no horizontal component of velocity (cos 90° = 0), so it simply goes straight up and comes straight down. At any of the other angles it has both components and moves in two dimensions.

q: At any point of its path, the velocity of a projectile is directed:
o: Along the tangent to the path at that point
Perpendicular to the path at that point
x: The velocity of any moving body points along the tangent to its path. For a projectile its direction changes continuously because the vertical component changes while the horizontal one stays fixed.

q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from the top of a high cliff. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², what is its speed 2 s later?
x: Horizontal component stays 15 m s⁻¹; vertical component = gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m s⁻¹. Speed = √(15² + 20²) = √625 = 25 m s⁻¹. Adding the components directly (35) ignores that they are at right angles.

q: In the absence of air resistance, the path followed by a projectile is a:
x: Horizontal distance grows in proportion to t while vertical displacement depends on t², so height is a quadratic function of horizontal distance. That curve is a parabola.

q: Once a projectile has left the thrower's hand, and air resistance is ignored, the only force acting on it is:
o: Its weight together with a forward force from the throw
A horizontal force that keeps it moving forward
No force at all, since it is moving freely
x: After release, the hand no longer pushes the projectile, so the only force is gravity (its weight). No forward force is needed to keep it moving horizontally, because the horizontal velocity simply stays constant.

q: A ball is projected from level ground and lands on the same level. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is correct?
o: The time taken to rise is greater than the time taken to fall
The time taken to rise to the highest point equals the time taken to fall back
The highest point is reached at the end of the range
The ball lands with a smaller speed than it was launched with
x: Without air resistance the path is symmetrical about the highest point: rise time equals fall time, the top is reached at half the range, and the ball lands with its launch speed.

q: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, with what speed does it land on the same level?
x: The horizontal component is unchanged and the vertical component returns with the same size but reversed, so the landing speed equals the launch speed, 20 m s⁻¹. 17.3 m s⁻¹ is only the horizontal component.

q: A ball is thrown at 45° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of its path the ball has:
o: Only a horizontal velocity, and an acceleration g downward
Zero velocity, and an acceleration g downward
Only a vertical velocity, and zero acceleration
x: At the top the vertical component of velocity is momentarily zero, but the horizontal component remains, so the velocity is horizontal. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g downward.

q: A projectile is launched from level ground at an angle θ above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, just before it lands its velocity makes an angle with the horizontal of:
o: Zero, since it is moving horizontally
x: The horizontal component is unchanged and the vertical component has the same size as at launch but points downward. So the landing velocity makes the same angle θ with the horizontal, now below it.

q: Compared with its ideal path with no air resistance, a cricket ball moving through real air, launched with the same speed and angle, has:
o: A greater range and a greater maximum height
The same range but a smaller maximum height
A smaller range and a smaller maximum height
The same maximum height but a smaller range
x: Air resistance opposes the motion and reduces both the horizontal and the vertical components of velocity. So the ball neither rises as high nor travels as far as the ideal parabola predicts.

q: A projectile is launched at 45° with speed v and no air resistance. With x horizontal and y vertical from the launch point, which equation describes its path?
x: Path: y = x tanθ − gx²/(2v² cos²θ). At 45°, tanθ = 1 and cos²θ = ½, so y = x − gx²/v². Forgetting the cos²θ term gives the version with 2v².

q: A ball is thrown at 60° above the horizontal from level ground. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy is least:
o: At the highest point of its path
Halfway up to its highest point
x: Speed is least at the top, where the vertical component is zero and only the horizontal component remains. The kinetic energy there is least but not zero, because the horizontal velocity is not zero.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal component of the velocity of a projectile during its flight:
o: Becomes zero at the highest point
x: No horizontal force acts on a projectile, so its horizontal velocity does not change. It is the vertical component that becomes zero at the highest point.

q: The horizontal component of a projectile's velocity stays constant because:
o: Its weight acts vertically, so there is no horizontal force on it
A horizontal force from the launch keeps acting on it
Its vertical motion cancels any change in the horizontal motion
Its acceleration is zero throughout the flight
x: By Newton's first law, velocity in a direction changes only if a force acts in that direction. Gravity is vertical, so the horizontal velocity is unchanged; the projectile still accelerates vertically, so its acceleration is not zero.

q: A ball is projected at 40 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its velocity at the highest point? (cos 60° = 0.5)
x: At the top only the horizontal component remains: 40 × cos 60° = 40 × 0.5 = 20 m s⁻¹. Using sin 60° gives 34.6 m s⁻¹, which is the initial vertical component.

q: The horizontal component of a projectile's velocity is 12 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, how far does it move horizontally in 3 s? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
x: Horizontal motion is uniform: x = vₓt = 12 × 3 = 36 m. Gravity does not affect it, so adding ½gt² (giving 81 m) is wrong.

q: An aeroplane flying horizontally at constant velocity releases a food packet. Ignoring air resistance, where is the packet relative to the aeroplane as it falls?
o: Further and further behind the aeroplane
Further and further ahead of the aeroplane
On a straight slanting line behind the aeroplane
x: The packet keeps the aeroplane's horizontal velocity, which stays constant. It therefore moves forward exactly as fast as the aeroplane and stays directly below it while falling.

q: A marble rolls off a horizontal table top at 3 m s⁻¹ and hits the floor 0.4 s later. Ignoring air resistance, how far from the foot of the table does it land? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
x: Horizontal distance = vₓt = 3 × 0.4 = 1.2 m. 0.8 m is the height of the table (½gt² = ½ × 10 × 0.16), not the horizontal distance.

q: For a projectile with no air resistance, a graph of the horizontal component of velocity against time is:
o: A straight line through the origin
x: The horizontal velocity does not change with time, so its graph is a horizontal line (zero slope). A downward-sloping line describes the vertical component.

q: A projectile launched at 60° above the horizontal has a speed of 15 m s⁻¹ at the highest point of its path. Ignoring air resistance, what was its launch speed? (cos 60° = 0.5)
x: Speed at the top equals the constant horizontal component: v cos 60° = 15, so v = 15 ÷ 0.5 = 30 m s⁻¹. Multiplying by 0.5 instead of dividing gives 7.5 m s⁻¹.

q: A passenger in a train moving at constant velocity on a straight track throws a ball vertically upward. Ignoring air resistance, an observer standing on the ground sees the ball:
o: Go straight up and come straight down
Follow a parabola and land back in the passenger's hand
x: The ball shares the train's horizontal velocity, which stays constant, so to the ground observer it moves forward while rising and falling, a parabola. Since ball and passenger move forward equally, it lands back in the hand.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the acceleration of a projectile at every point of its path is:
o: g, along the direction of its velocity
Different at different points of the path
x: The only force is the weight, which is constant and vertical, so the acceleration is always g downward. It is not along the velocity, which changes direction during the flight.

q: A ball is thrown at 45° above the horizontal. Taking upward as positive and g = 10 m s⁻², its vertical acceleration while rising and while falling is:
o: −10 m s⁻² while rising and +10 m s⁻² while falling
+10 m s⁻² while rising and −10 m s⁻² while falling
−10 m s⁻² while rising and −10 m s⁻² while falling
Zero while rising and −10 m s⁻² while falling
x: Gravity always pulls downward, so the vertical acceleration is −10 m s⁻² throughout. While rising it slows the ball; while falling it speeds it up, but its direction never changes.

q: From the same height and at the same instant, one ball is dropped from rest and an identical ball is thrown horizontally. Ignoring air resistance, which reaches the level ground first?
o: It depends on how fast the second ball is thrown
Both reach the ground at the same time
x: Both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so they take the same time to fall the same height. The horizontal velocity does not affect the vertical motion.

q: Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the vertical component of a projectile's velocity changes by:
o: 10 m s⁻¹ downward in every second
5 m s⁻¹ downward in every second
x: An acceleration of 10 m s⁻² means velocity changes by 10 m s⁻¹ each second, here in the downward direction. 10 m is a distance, not a change of velocity; it is the horizontal component that stays constant.

q: A 2 kg ball and a 5 kg ball are projected with the same velocity. Ignoring air resistance, their accelerations during the flight are:
x: The weight mg is the only force, so a = mg ÷ m = g for any mass. Both balls fall with the same acceleration, like freely falling bodies.

q: Ignoring air resistance, which of these quantities stays the same throughout the flight of a projectile?
o: The vertical component of its velocity
x: The acceleration is always g downward. Speed, the vertical velocity and the direction of the velocity all change as the projectile rises and falls.

q: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal and lands on the same level. Ignoring air resistance, what is the change in its velocity from launch to landing? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5)
x: The vertical component goes from +10 m s⁻¹ to −10 m s⁻¹, a change of 20 m s⁻¹ downward; the horizontal component is unchanged. Check: time of flight 2 s, and gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m s⁻¹. The speed is the same, but velocity is not.

q: A ball is thrown at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is the angle between its velocity and its acceleration at the highest point?
x: At the top the velocity is horizontal and the acceleration g is vertically downward, so they are at right angles. At launch the angle between them is 120°, not 30°.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the vertical motion of a projectile is exactly the same as the motion of:
o: A body moving horizontally at constant speed
A body sliding down a smooth inclined plane
A body thrown straight up with the projectile's full launch speed
A body thrown straight up with a speed equal to the projectile's initial vertical component
x: Vertically, a projectile starts with v sinθ and has acceleration g downward, just like a body thrown straight up at v sinθ. Using the full launch speed would only be right for a 90° launch.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal motion of a projectile has an acceleration of:
x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal acceleration is zero. The acceleration g belongs only to the vertical motion.

q: A projectile is launched with speed v at angle θ above the horizontal. Which pair gives its horizontal distance x and its height y after time t?
o: x = (v sinθ)t and y = (v cosθ)t − ½gt²
x = (v cosθ)t − ½gt² and y = (v sinθ)t
x = (v cosθ)t and y = (v sinθ)t − ½gt²
x = (v cosθ)t and y = (v sinθ)t + ½gt²
x: Horizontally the motion is uniform with vₓ = v cosθ. Vertically it starts at v sinθ upward with acceleration g downward, so y = (v sinθ)t − ½gt².

q: Which statement correctly describes the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile?
o: The vertical motion gradually slows the horizontal motion
They are independent: each takes place as if the other were absent
The horizontal motion reduces the vertical acceleration
Both motions have the same acceleration
x: Horizontal and vertical motions do not affect each other; they share only the time. The horizontal acceleration is zero and the vertical acceleration is g, so they are not the same.

q: Taking upward as positive, the graph of the vertical component of a projectile's velocity against time is:
o: A straight line with a negative slope equal to −g
A straight line with a positive slope equal to +g
x: vᵧ = v sinθ − gt, which is a straight line decreasing at the rate g. A horizontal line describes the horizontal component; a parabola describes the height against time.

q: For a projectile, the horizontal displacement is directly proportional to time. Its vertical displacement:
o: Is also directly proportional to t
Depends on both t and t²
x: x = (v cosθ)t is linear in t, but y = (v sinθ)t − ½gt² contains a t² term because the vertical motion is accelerated.

q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. What are the initial horizontal and vertical components of its velocity? (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2)
o: 10 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 10√3 m s⁻¹ vertical
10√3 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 10 m s⁻¹ vertical
20 m s⁻¹ horizontal and zero vertical
10 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 10 m s⁻¹ vertical
x: Horizontal = 20 cos 30° = 20 × √3/2 = 10√3 m s⁻¹ (about 17.3); vertical = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. Swapping sin and cos gives the reverse pair.

q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a high tower. Ignoring air resistance (g = 10 m s⁻²), after what time does its velocity make an angle of 45° with the horizontal?
x: At 45° the vertical and horizontal components are equal: gt = 10 m s⁻¹, so t = 10 ÷ 10 = 1 s. The horizontal component stays 10 m s⁻¹ throughout.

q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from a cliff top. Ignoring air resistance (g = 10 m s⁻²), how far has it moved horizontally and vertically after 1 s?
o: 10 m horizontally and no distance down
x: x = vₓt = 10 × 1 = 10 m; y = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 1² = 5 m down. Forgetting the ½ gives 10 m down.

q: When solving a projectile problem, the quantity that links the horizontal motion to the vertical motion is:
o: The acceleration, which is the same for both motions
The velocity, which is the same for both motions
The displacement, which is the same for both motions
The time, which is the same for both motions
x: Both motions last exactly as long as the flight, so time is common to them. Their accelerations (zero and g), velocities and displacements are generally different.

q: A projectile is launched from level ground with speed v at angle θ. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal range R on the same level is:
x: Range = horizontal velocity × time of flight = v cosθ × 2v sinθ/g = v² sin2θ/g. v² sin²θ/2g is the maximum height and 2v sinθ/g is the time of flight.

q: Ignoring air resistance, at what launch angle does a projectile fired from level ground with a given speed have its maximum range?
x: R = v² sin2θ/g is largest when sin2θ = 1, that is 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°. At 90° the range is zero.

q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what maximum height does it reach? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5)
x: H = v² sin²θ / 2g = 400 × 0.25 / 20 = 5 m. Forgetting to square sin 30° gives 10 m; 20 m is the height for a vertical throw.

q: A ball is projected from level ground at 40 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, how long is it in the air? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87)
x: T = 2v sinθ / g = 2 × 40 × 0.5 / 10 = 4 s. 2 s is only the time to reach the top; 6.9 s comes from using cos 30° instead of sin 30°.

q: A stone is projected from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at 15° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its range? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5, sin 60° ≈ 0.87)
x: R = v² sin2θ / g = 400 × sin 30° / 10 = 400 × 0.5 / 10 = 20 m. Note it is sin 2θ, so with θ = 15° we need sin 30°.

q: A ball projected from level ground at 30° above the horizontal has range R. At what other launch angle, with the same speed, will it have the same range?
x: R depends on sin2θ, and sin 60° = sin 120°, so 30° and 60° give equal ranges. Any two complementary angles (adding to 90°) give the same range.

q: What is the maximum range on level ground of a ball that can be thrown at 30 m s⁻¹? Ignore air resistance and take g = 10 m s⁻².
x: Maximum range occurs at 45°, where sin 90° = 1: R = v²/g = 900/10 = 90 m. 45 m is v²/2g, the height reached in a vertical throw.

q: Two balls are projected with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is the ratio of the maximum height of the 30° ball to that of the 60° ball?
x: H ∝ sin²θ: sin²30° : sin²60° = ¼ : ¾ = 1 : 3. Their ranges are equal (complementary angles), but their heights are not.

q: A projectile is launched at the angle that gives maximum range R on level ground. Ignoring air resistance, its maximum height is:
x: At 45°, R = v²/g and H = v² sin²45° / 2g = v² × ½ / 2g = v²/4g. So H = R/4.

q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, where is it 1 s after launch? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87)
x: x = (20 × 0.87) × 1 = 17.4 m; y = (20 × 0.5) × 1 − ½ × 10 × 1² = 10 − 5 = 5 m. Forgetting the ½gt² term gives 10 m up.

q: A projectile's launch speed is doubled while its launch angle stays the same. Ignoring air resistance, its range and its time of flight become:
x: R = v² sin2θ/g is proportional to v², so it becomes 4 times; T = 2v sinθ/g is proportional to v, so it doubles.
